hypotheses.title: CLPool.initialize callable by anyone on uninitialized clone
hypotheses.description: `initialize` only checks `factory == address(0) && _factory != address(0)`. It does not verify that `msg.sender` is the factory (or that `_factory` matches the real factory). Because pools are deployed as EIP-1167 clones via `Clones.cloneDeterministic`, the clone address is publicly computable from `(token0, token1, tickSpacing)` before the factory calls `initialize`. An attacker can front-run the factory's `createPool` call and call `initialize` directly on the freshly cloned pool with attacker-chosen `_factory`, `_token0`, `_token1`, `_tickSpacing`, `_gaugeManager`, and `_sqrtPriceX96`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes/derives the deterministic clone address for a desired pool (or simply watches the mempool for `createPool`). 2) Attacker calls `CLPool(pool).initialize(attackerFactory, attackerToken0, attackerToken1, tickSpacing, attackerGaugeManager, attackerPrice)` before the factory's `createPool` transaction executes. 3) The factory's subsequent `initialize` reverts (factory != 0), but the pool is now permanently bound to attacker-controlled `factory`, `token0`, `token1`, and `gaugeManager`. 4) Attacker's fake factory can return arbitrary `getSwapFee`, `getUnstakedFee`, `getProtocolFee` values, and the attacker's `gaugeManager` can later call `setGaugeAndPositionManager` to install a malicious gauge/nft.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of the pool's configuration: arbitrary fee extraction, ability to set gauge/nft to attacker contracts, and full control over protocol fee routing. Users interacting with the pool lose funds to attacker-controlled fee logic.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == _factory` (or `msg.sender == poolImplementation`'s deployer) in `initialize`, and/or have the factory pass a one-time initialization token. Alternatively, initialize inside the factory's `createPool` atomically via a constructor-like pattern.

hypotheses.title: GaugeManager.initialize callable by anyone (unprotected initializer)
hypotheses.description: `GaugeManager` inherits `OwnableUpgradeable` and `ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable` and uses the `initializer` modifier, but the contract is deployed directly (constructor is empty) rather than behind a proxy in the provided code. The `initializer` modifier only prevents re-initialization of the same instance; it does not restrict who may call `initialize` the first time. Any external actor can call `initialize` on a freshly deployed `GaugeManager` before the legitimate deployer does, setting `_ve`, `tokenHandler`, factories, `permissionRegistry`, and `nfpm` to attacker-controlled addresses and becoming the owner.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors deployment of `GaugeManager`. 2) Attacker front-runs the legitimate `initialize` transaction and calls `initialize(attackerVe, attackerTokenHandler, attackerGaugeFactory, attackerGaugeFactoryCL, attackerPairFactory, attackerPairFactoryCL, attackerPermReg, attackerNfpm)`. 3) Attacker becomes `owner()` and controls `permissionRegistry`, so `GaugeAdmin`/`Governance` modifiers resolve to attacker-controlled roles. 4) Attacker can then call `setMinter`, `setVoter`, `setBribeFactory`, `addGaugeFactory`, etc.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of the gauge system: attacker can mint/distribute rewards arbitrarily, create malicious gauges, redirect bribes, and drain `base` tokens held by the manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(msg.sender == _initializer)` or restrict `initialize` to a deployer-set address, or deploy behind a proxy and call `initialize` atomically in the proxy constructor.

hypotheses.title: GaugeManager.distributeAll iterates unbounded pools array, DoS on reward distribution
hypotheses.description: `distributeAll()` loops over `pools.length` with no upper bound and calls `_distribute` for each gauge, which in turn calls `IGauge(_gauge).notifyRewardAmount` / `IGaugeCL(_gauge).notifyRewardAmount`. Any single gauge that reverts (e.g., a CL gauge whose `notifyRewardAmount` reverts due to `require(rewardRate <= contractBalance / epochTimeRemaining)` or a malicious/broken gauge) causes the entire loop to revert, blocking distribution for all other gauges. Since `pools` grows monotonically via `_saveBribeData` and is never pruned, the array can grow arbitrarily large, making the loop both gas-unbounded and permanently revertible.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates many gauges (or a single gauge whose `notifyRewardAmount` reverts, e.g., by manipulating reward token balance/rate). 2) Attacker calls `distributeAll()` or relies on the minter/keeper flow. 3) The loop reverts on the malicious gauge, so no gauge receives emissions for that epoch. 4) Even without a malicious gauge, once `pools.length` is large enough, the loop exceeds block gas limit and `distributeAll()` becomes uncallable.
hypotheses.impact: Emissions distribution is frozen for all gauges; users cannot receive rewards; protocol emissions are stuck in GaugeManager; the `distributeAll` path is permanently DoS'd.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the paginated `distribute(start, finish)` variant as the primary path, or wrap each `_distribute` call in a try/catch and skip failing gauges; also cap `pools.length` or prune dead gauges.

hypotheses.title: Missing access control on initialize() allows anyone to hijack CLPool
hypotheses.description: `initialize()` only checks `factory == address(0)` and `_factory != address(0)`, with no restriction that `msg.sender` must be the factory (or the pool itself via the clone deployer). Because `Clones.cloneDeterministic` deploys the clone and then the factory calls `initialize`, an attacker can front-run the factory's `initialize` call on the freshly deployed clone (or call it directly on any uninitialized clone from CLFactory's `poolImplementation`), setting attacker-controlled `_token0`, `_token1`, `_gaugeManager`, and `_sqrtPriceX96`. The factory's subsequent call would revert (factory already set), permanently locking the intended pool configuration.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes pending `createPool` tx (or simply predicts the deterministic clone address via `Clones.predictDeterministicAddress`). 2) Attacker calls `initialize(attacker, tokenA, tokenB, tickSpacing, attacker, manipulatedPrice)` on the clone before the factory does. 3) Factory's own `initialize` reverts because `factory != address(0)`. 4) All future `mint`, `swap` calls use attacker-controlled token/gauge/price settings; subsequent factory mapping writes (`getPool[...]`) point to a maliciously-initialized pool.
hypotheses.impact: Full loss of user funds sent to the pool, poisoned swap pricing, malicious gauge hookups, and committed factory state pointing at an attacker-controlled pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initialize` to `msg.sender == factory` (or `require(factory == address(0) && msg.sender == _factory)`).

hypotheses.title: CLPool.setGaugeAndPositionManager callable by gaugeManager without gauge validation
hypotheses.description: The function only checks `msg.sender == gaugeManager && gauge == address(0)`. `gaugeManager` is set during `initialize` from the `_gaugeManager` argument. If `initialize` is front-run (see previous finding) or if the factory's `gaugeManager` is ever set to an attacker-controlled address, the attacker can set `gauge` and `nft` to arbitrary contracts. Even without front-running, the check does not verify that `_gauge` is a legitimate gauge deployed by the GaugeManager, nor that `_nft` is the canonical NonfungiblePositionManager.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains control of `gaugeManager` (via front-run initialize, or if the factory's `gaugeManager` is misconfigured/upgraded). 2) Attacker calls `setGaugeAndPositionManager(maliciousGauge, maliciousNft)`. 3) `onlyGauge`-protected functions (`stake`, `collectFees`, `syncReward`, `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal`) now trust the malicious gauge. 4) `onlyNftManager`-protected `collect`/`burn` overloads now trust the malicious nft, allowing it to drain any position's `tokensOwed`.
hypotheses.impact: Malicious gauge can call `collectFees` to drain `gaugeFees`, `syncReward` to manipulate reward accounting, and `stake` to corrupt `stakedLiquidity`. Malicious nft can call `collect(..., owner)` and `burn(..., owner)` for arbitrary owners, stealing all accrued fees from any LP position.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `_gauge` against `IGaugeManager(gaugeManager).isGauge(_gauge)` and `_nft` against the canonical NFPM address stored at initialization; also require `msg.sender == factory` for this one-time setter.

hypotheses.title: GaugeManager.distributeFees unbounded loop over pools blocks fee collection
hypotheses.description: `distributeFees()` iterates over the entire `pools` array and calls `_distributeFees` for each, which invokes `IGauge(gauges[_pool]).claimFees()` or `IGaugeCL(...).claimFees()`. Any gauge whose `claimFees` reverts (e.g., a CL gauge whose `clPool.collectFees()` reverts, or a bribe whose `notifyRewardAmount` reverts) will revert the whole loop. Because `pools` is append-only and never pruned, the loop is also gas-unbounded and will eventually exceed the block gas limit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a gauge whose `claimFees` reverts (e.g., by making the internal bribe reject `notifyRewardAmount`, or by draining/blocking the pool's fee transfer). 2) Anyone calling `distributeFees()` reverts. 3) Fees accumulate in gauges and are never forwarded to bribes.
hypotheses.impact: LP fee distribution to bribes is permanently blocked; fees stuck in gauge contracts; voters receive no fee rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the paginated `distributeFees(start, finish)` variant, wrap each call in try/catch, and prune dead gauges from `pools`.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL.withdraw blocked when emergency mode is active, trapping staked NFTs
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` is guarded by `isNotEmergency`, so when the owner activates emergency mode, users cannot withdraw their staked NFT positions. The only escape is `emergencyWithdraw` in `GaugeV2`, but `GaugeCL` has no equivalent emergency withdrawal function. Once `activateEmergencyMode()` is called, staked CL positions are permanently locked in the gauge until the owner calls `stopEmergencyMode()`, which is a trusted-only action.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner (or a compromised owner key) calls `activateEmergencyMode()`. 2) Users attempt `withdraw(tokenId, redeemType)` and it reverts with "emergency". 3) There is no user-callable path to retrieve the NFT; funds are frozen.
hypotheses.impact: Users' staked NFT positions (and the underlying liquidity) are frozen indefinitely; loss of access to funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a user-callable `emergencyWithdraw(tokenId)` in `GaugeCL` that transfers the NFT back without reward accrual, mirroring `GaugeV2.emergencyWithdraw`.

hypotheses.title: HybrSwapper.swapToHYBR trusts arbitrary aggregator calldata
hypotheses.description: `swapToHYBR` approves `params.aggregator` to spend `params.amountIn` of `params.tokenIn` and then executes `params.aggregator.call(params.callData)` with no validation of the calldata. The aggregator is whitelisted by owner, but the calldata is fully attacker-controlled. A malicious or compromised whitelisted aggregator (or a whitelisted aggregator with a vulnerable function) can be invoked with calldata that transfers the approved tokens to an attacker, or that re-enters `swapToHYBR` (nonReentrant prevents re-entry into this function, but the aggregator can call other functions). More directly, since `params.tokenIn` is attacker-chosen and the contract approves the aggregator for `amountIn`, an attacker can pass a `tokenIn` that is a token the contract holds (e.g., HYBR is forbidden, but other tokens held by the contract are not) and have the aggregator drain them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `swapToHYBR` with `tokenIn` = any ERC20 the HybrSwapper holds (e.g., leftover tokens from previous swaps), `amountIn` = balance, `aggregator` = whitelisted aggregator, `callData` = `transferFrom(swapper, attacker, amount)`. 2) The aggregator executes the transfer, draining the contract. 3) `hybrReceived` is 0, but `minAmountOut` can be set to 0 to bypass the slippage check.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of any ERC20 tokens held by HybrSwapper (other than HYBR, which is explicitly forbidden as tokenIn but can still be drained via a different tokenIn path if the aggregator's calldata targets HYBR).
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `params.tokenIn` is the expected input token and that the aggregator's calldata targets only the intended swap; consider using a strict interface instead of arbitrary `call`.

hypotheses.title: GovernanceHYBR.withdraw splits veNFT with fee amount = 0
hypotheses.description: In `withdraw`, the code builds `amounts` of length 3: [remainingAmount, userAmount, feeAmount]. `multiSplit` requires every entry > 0 ("ZW"), but the default `withdrawFee` is 100 (1%) and can be set down to `MIN_WITHDRAW_FEE = 10`; if `hybrAmount * withdrawFee / BASIS == 0` (e.g., small shares), `feeAmount` becomes 0 and `multiSplit` reverts. More importantly, the contract calls `multiSplit(veTokenId, amounts)` while it is the owner of the veNFT — but `withdraw` already `_burn`s user shares before splitting, so a revert here leaves the user shares burned without receiving the NFT (state partially applied only via burn; subsequent calls would use the reduced totalSupply). Additionally, the contract computes `remainingAmount = veBalance - userAmount - feeAmount` using `veBalance = totalAssets()` which after previous withdraws may not equal the sum of the split amounts, causing an accounting mismatch in subsequent `calculateAssets`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `withdraw(shares)` with `shares` such that `calculateAssets(shares) * withdrawFee / 10000 == 0` (dust withdrawal, e.g., 1 wei). `_burn(msg.sender, shares)` succeeds, then `multiSplit` reverts with "ZW". The user's gHYBR shares are burned with no NFT returned; `totalSupply` is permanently reduced, and `totalAssets()` no longer maps proportionally to remaining shares — value leaks to remaining holders. A user could also repeatedly trigger this to grief the accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user funds (burned shares without withdrawal) and inflated per-share value for remaining holders since totalSupply decreases without totalAssets decreasing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `feeAmount > 0` (or omit the third NFT when fee is 0), and compute amounts from the actual veNFT balance atomically before burning shares; consider a separate "collectFee" path.

hypotheses.title: CLPool.swap lacks a minimum-out / slippage parameter for the caller
hypotheses.description: `swap` accepts `amountSpecified` and `sqrtPriceLimitX96` but no `amountOutMinimum` (or `amountInMaximum` for exact-output). The only protection is the price limit, which is a coarse bound. A caller (e.g., a router or an integrating contract) that does not independently enforce a minimum output can be sandwiched: an attacker moves the price within the allowed limit, the victim's swap executes at the manipulated price, and the attacker reverses the move. The pool itself provides no slippage guard.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim submits a swap with a wide `sqrtPriceLimitX96` (or the router's default MIN/MAX). 2) Attacker front-runs with a large swap to move the price toward the limit. 3) Victim's swap executes at the worse price. 4) Attacker back-runs to restore the price and pockets the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Victims receive less output than expected; value extracted by sandwich attackers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `amountOutMinimum` (exact-input) / `amountInMaximum` (exact-output) parameter to `swap` and enforce it before returning, or require all callers to use a router that enforces it (and document that the pool alone is unsafe).

hypotheses.title: delegateBySig missing chainId in domain separator
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 domain separator is built with `DOMAIN_TYPEHASH = keccak256("EIP712Domain(string name,uint256 chainId,address verifyingContract)")` (3 fields) but the actual `abi.encode` call passes 5 arguments: DOMAIN_TYPEHASH, nameHash, versionHash, block.chainid, address(this). The typehash does not include `version`, so the encoded struct does not match the declared typehash. More importantly, the domain separator is computed inline on every call rather than cached, and the typehash omits the version field that is actually being hashed — meaning the digest is not a valid EIP-712 digest and the same signature can be replayed on any chain where the contract is deployed at the same address (since chainId is included but the typehash mismatch means wallets/signers compute a different digest than the contract, and any signature that happens to verify is chain-agnostic in practice if the contract is deployed via CREATE2 at the same address). The nonce is incremented only after `ecrecover` succeeds, but the digest construction is malformed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid `delegateBySig` signature on chain A. 2) If the same VotingEscrow is deployed at the same address on chain B (common with deterministic deploys), the attacker replays the exact same (v,r,s,nonce,expiry,delegatee) on chain B. 3) Because the domain separator is recomputed with chain B's chainId, the digest differs — but the typehash mismatch means the signer's off-chain computed digest (using the standard 4-field EIP-712 domain) also differs, so any signature that verifies on chain A will not verify on chain B. However, the real issue is that the typehash declares 3 fields while 5 are encoded, so the digest is non-standard and signers cannot reliably produce valid signatures; any signature that does verify is effectively replayable across any context where the same malformed digest is produced.
hypotheses.impact: Delegation signatures can be replayed or, conversely, legitimate signatures fail to verify, leading to unauthorized delegation or denial of delegation. If a signature is crafted to match the malformed digest, it can be reused across chains/contracts at the same address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a standard EIP-712 domain typehash that matches the encoded fields, e.g. `keccak256("EIP712Domain(string name,string version,uint256 chainId,address verifyingContract)")`, and cache the domain separator with chainId invalidation.

hypotheses.title: GrowthHYBR.receivePenaltyReward is permissionless and mints veNFT
hypotheses.description: `receivePenaltyReward(amount)` is external with no access control. It calls `IERC20(HYBR).approve(votingEscrow, amount)` and then either initializes a veNFT or calls `deposit_for(veTokenId, amount)`. The function assumes `amount` of HYBR has already been transferred to the contract (by RewardHYBR's `_redeemToHYBR`). However, any external caller can invoke `receivePenaltyReward` with an arbitrary `amount` as long as the contract holds HYBR. Since the contract holds HYBR from user deposits and rewards, an attacker can call `receivePenaltyReward` to force the contract to lock its HYBR into the veNFT, potentially locking funds that were meant for withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes GrowthHYBR holds HYBR (e.g., from a user deposit or penalty reward). 2) Attacker calls `receivePenaltyReward(amount)` with `amount` up to the contract's HYBR balance. 3) The contract approves and deposits the HYBR into the veNFT, locking it for MAX_LOCK_DURATION. 4) Users attempting to withdraw may find insufficient liquid HYBR, or the contract's accounting (`penalty` variable) is inflated.
hypotheses.impact: Forced locking of contract HYBR, potentially blocking withdrawals and corrupting `penalty` accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `receivePenaltyReward` to the RewardHYBR contract (or a trusted set of callers) via an access control check.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.delegateBySig missing signatory != delegatee check and nonce replay via nonce increment
hypotheses.description: `delegateBySig` checks `delegatee != msg.sender` and `delegatee != address(0)`, but does not check that `signatory != delegatee`. More importantly, the nonce is incremented via `nonces[signatory]++` inside the `require` expression, which means the increment happens even if the subsequent `require(block.timestamp <= expiry)` fails — but that is a minor issue. The real issue is that the EIP-712 domain separator uses `keccak256(bytes(name))` and `keccak256(bytes(version))` where `name` and `version` are `string constant` — this is fine. However, the function does not verify that `signatory` is not the zero address before incrementing the nonce (it does check `signatory != address(0)` after `ecrecover`, but the nonce increment happens in the same `require` as the nonce check, so a zero-address signatory would increment `nonces[address(0)]`). More critically, there is no check that `signatory != delegatee`, allowing a user to delegate to themselves via signature (harmless) — but the missing check that the recovered signatory actually owns any veNFT means anyone can delegate on behalf of any address that has ever signed a delegation message, which is intended. The actual vulnerability is that `nonces[signatory]++` is evaluated before the expiry check, so an expired signature still consumes a nonce.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a signed delegation message from a victim (e.g., from a failed transaction or a phishing attempt). 2) Attacker submits `delegateBySig` with an expired `expiry`. 3) The `require(nonce == nonces[signatory]++)` passes and increments the nonce, then `require(block.timestamp <= expiry)` reverts. 4) The victim's nonce is now incremented, invalidating any other pending valid signatures the victim may have.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: attacker can invalidate a victim's pending valid delegation signatures by submitting expired ones, forcing the victim to re-sign. No direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the expiry check before the nonce increment, and use a local variable for the nonce check.

hypotheses.title: DynamicSwapFeeModule uses spot tick instead of TWAP for current price
hypotheses.description: The dynamic fee is computed as `absTickDelta = |currentTick - twAvgTick|` where `currentTick` is read directly from `slot0()` (the instantaneous spot tick). An attacker can manipulate the spot tick within a single transaction (e.g., via a large swap in the same pool or a flash-loan-funded swap) to inflate the tick delta, which raises the swap fee applied to the very next swap in the same block. Because the fee is applied to the attacker's own subsequent swap, the attacker can grief other users or sandwich them with an artificially high fee.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker flash-loans tokens and performs a large swap in the pool to push `slot0.tick` far from the TWAP. 2) In the same transaction, the attacker (or a victim's pending swap) triggers `getFee`, which now returns a much higher fee due to the inflated `absTickDelta`. 3) The victim's swap pays the inflated fee; the attacker reverses the price move and pockets the difference or simply griefs.
hypotheses.impact: Victims pay inflated swap fees; fee accounting is manipulated by spot-price manipulation within a single block.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the TWAP tick itself (or a bounded deviation) as the reference for the current price, or require the spot tick to be within a tolerance of the TWAP before applying the dynamic component.

hypotheses.title: OracleLibrary.consult can return a manipulated TWAP if cardinality is low
hypotheses.description: `consult` computes the arithmetic mean tick over `secondsAgo` using `observe`. If the pool's `observationCardinality` is low (e.g., 1, the default at initialization), `observe` will revert for any `secondsAgo` older than the single stored observation, or will return a value derived from a very short window. An attacker can manipulate the spot price and, if the oracle has not been grown, the TWAP over the requested window is effectively the manipulated spot price. Integrators that rely on `consult` without checking `observationCardinality` can be fed a manipulated price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a pool with low `observationCardinality` (common for newly created pools). 2) Attacker flash-loans and swaps to move the spot price. 3) Attacker calls an integrator that uses `OracleLibrary.consult` with a short `secondsAgo`; the returned TWAP reflects the manipulated price. 4) Integrator acts on the wrong price (e.g., liquidates, mints, or swaps at a bad rate). 5) Attacker reverses the price move.
hypotheses.impact: Integrators using `consult` on low-cardinality pools can be manipulated into wrong pricing decisions, leading to loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `observationCardinality` to be sufficiently large (e.g., >= secondsAgo / MIN_SECONDS_AGO) before trusting `consult`, or use `getOldestObservationSecondsAgo` to validate the window.

hypotheses.title: CLPool.swap reentrancy via swap callback before slot0.unlocked reset
hypotheses.description: The swap function sets `slot0.unlocked = false` at the start but only resets it to `true` at the very end, after the `uniswapV3SwapCallback` external call. However, the callback is invoked while the pool state (slot0, feeGrowthGlobal, gaugeFees, protocolFees, liquidity) has already been updated. A malicious callback can re-enter other pool functions that do not use the `lock` modifier — specifically `collectFees`, `collectProtocolFees`, `setGaugeAndPositionManager`, `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal`, `syncReward`, `stake`, and `collect` (which uses `lock` but the lock is already held). More critically, the callback can call `swap` again on a different pool or the same pool via a nested path, and since `slot0.unlocked` is false, the nested `swap` will revert — but the callback can still call `collect`/`collectFees`/`stake` which are `lock`-guarded and will revert too. The real issue is that `collectFees` and `collectProtocolFees` are `lock`-guarded but `collectProtocolFees` is callable by factory only. The exploitable path is that during the swap callback, the attacker can call `flash` on the same pool — `flash` uses `lock` so it reverts. The actual reentrancy vector is that `swap` does not use the `lock` modifier at all; it manually manages `slot0.unlocked`. This means a callback can call `mint`/`burn`/`collect` which check `slot0.unlocked` and revert. So the direct reentrancy is blocked. However, the callback can call `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` (lock-guarded, reverts) or `syncReward` (lock-guarded, reverts). The genuine issue: `swap` updates `slot0.sqrtPriceX96` and `slot0.tick` BEFORE the callback, and the callback can read these updated values via `slot0()` and `observe()` to perform read-only reentrancy against external protocols that trust the pool's price. Since `slot0.unlocked` is false during the callback, external integrators checking `unlocked` would be protected, but many do not check it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract that calls `pool.swap(...)` with a callback. 2. Inside `uniswapV3SwapCallback`, the attacker reads `pool.slot0()` which now reflects the post-swap price but the swap is not yet finalized (payment not verified). 3. The attacker uses this manipulated price to interact with a third-party protocol (e.g., a lending market) that reads the pool price without checking `unlocked`. 4. The attacker extracts value from the third-party protocol based on the transient price.
hypotheses.impact: Read-only reentrancy allows manipulation of external protocols that consume CLPool price data, potentially causing loss of funds in integrators.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the `lock` modifier to `swap` or ensure all external integrators check `slot0.unlocked`; alternatively, update `slot0` only after the callback completes.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL.deposit blocked in emergency, preventing new stakes but also blocking reward claims
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` is guarded by `isNotEmergency`. While this is intended to stop new stakes, it also means that during emergency mode no new positions can be added, and combined with the `withdraw` guard, the gauge becomes fully inert for users. More importantly, `getReward` is callable via `GaugeManager.claimRewards` but `_getReward` calls `_updateRewards` which calls `clPool.updateRewardsGrowthGlobal()` — if the pool's `lastUpdated` logic or reward reserve is in a bad state, claims can revert. The emergency flag effectively freezes the gauge's user-facing surface.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner activates emergency. 2) Users cannot deposit or withdraw. 3) Reward claims via `getReward` may still work but the NFT is stuck. 4) If owner never deactivates, users are locked out.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot manage positions; gauge becomes unusable; potential permanent lock if owner is unavailable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow withdrawals during emergency (only block deposits), or provide a separate emergency exit path.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw blocked by voted/attachments flags, funds can be frozen by voter
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` requires `attachments[_tokenId] == 0 && !voted[_tokenId]`. These flags are set by the `voter` contract via `voting()` and `attach()`. If the voter contract is compromised, buggy, or simply fails to call `abstain`/`detach` (e.g., due to a revert in the voter's reset path), the user's veNFT is permanently locked and the underlying HYBR cannot be withdrawn even after the lock expires. There is no user-callable override to clear these flags.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User votes via voter, setting `voted[tokenId] = true`. 2) Voter's `reset` path reverts or is disabled (e.g., due to a bug or governance action). 3) User's lock expires but `withdraw` reverts with "ATT". 4) Funds are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Locked HYBR is permanently frozen; user cannot recover principal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a time-based escape hatch (e.g., allow withdraw after lock expiry regardless of `voted` if the voter has not cleared it within N epochs), or ensure the voter's reset path is always callable.

hypotheses.title: RewardHYBR.redeemFor burns caller's tokens but credits arbitrary recipient
hypotheses.description: `redeemFor(amount, redeemType, recipient)` burns `amount` from `msg.sender` and then calls `_redeem(amount, redeemType, recipient)`, sending the redeemed HYBR/veNFT/gHYBR to an arbitrary `recipient` chosen by the caller. This is intended, but combined with `_redeemToVeHYBR` which calls `IVotingEscrow(votingEscrow).create_lock_for(amount, lockTime, recipient)`, an attacker can mint a veNFT directly to any address. More critically, `_redeemToHYBR` transfers `penalty` to `gHYBR` and calls `IGHYBR(gHYBR).receivePenaltyReward(penalty)` — but `gHYBR` is set by owner and `receivePenaltyReward` is permissionless, so anyone can call it directly with arbitrary amounts if they can get HYBR into the contract. The signature-relevant flaw is that `redeemFor` has no authorization tying `recipient` to `msg.sender`, allowing an attacker who controls any rHYBR balance to force-lock HYBR into a veNFT owned by a victim (griefing) or to redirect rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires a small amount of rHYBR (e.g., via gauge rewards). 2) Calls `redeemFor(amount, 1, victimAddress)` to create a veNFT locked for MAX_LOCK_DURATION owned by the victim. 3) Victim is now forced to hold a locked veNFT they did not request, and the attacker can repeat to spam victim's NFT list. Alternatively, attacker calls `redeemFor(amount, 0, attackerAddress)` to extract HYBR at the fixed rate.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing via forced veNFT creation on arbitrary addresses; potential reward redirection if recipient is a contract that mis-handles the NFT.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `redeemFor` to a whitelist of authorized callers (e.g., gauges) or require `recipient == msg.sender` unless caller is a trusted gauge.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow multiSplit loses remainder and can over-mint voting power
hypotheses.description: `multiSplit` allocates `amount: int128(uint256(int256(originalLocked.amount)) * amounts[i] / totalWeight)` per new NFT. Integer division truncates, so the sum of the split amounts can be strictly less than `originalLocked.amount`, effectively burning dust — but more importantly the original NFT is burned and `_checkpoint` is called with the zero locked balance, and then each new NFT is checked in with its share. If any single share rounds to zero, `_createSplitNFT` still mints an NFT with amount 0 and checkpointed with bias/slope 0, but `permanentLockBalance` is not adjusted for that zero-share. Conversely, because `permanentLockBalance` is only mutated in deposit/increase/lockPermanent/unlockPermanent/merge, splitting a permanent-locked NFT in `multiSplit` does not touch `permanentLockBalance`, so total `permanentLockBalance` remains equal to the original amount while locked amounts across the new NFTs sum to less. This breaks the `permanentLockBalance == sum of permanent locked amounts` invariant used by `totalSupplyAtT` via `point_history.permanent`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a permanent-locked veNFT of amount N. 2) Calls `multiSplit(_from, [1, 1])` (two shares). Sum of new amounts may be N or N-1 depending on rounding. `permanentLockBalance` still equals N. 3) `totalSupplyAtT` reads `point_history[epoch].permanent` which is set to `permanentLockBalance` in `_checkpoint` after each split; the new NFTs' `u_new.permanent` values are each set to `uint(int256(new_locked.amount))` in the user checkpoint but the global `permanent` is reset to `permanentLockBalance`. 4) Because global total voting supply includes `permanentLockBalance` (which exceeds actual locked), `totalSupply` is overstated, diluting other voters' RewardsDistributor claim shares. 5) Or, by repeated splits with weights that trivially zero out a share, attacker can craft a discrepancy N vs N-k for any k, allowing them to shift rewards between the RewardsDistributor and themselves. Any external actor can call multiSplit on their own NFT.
hypotheses.impact: Overstated total voting supply dilutes `RewardsDistributor` claims for all veNFT holders. Attacker can also cause per-NFT amounts to underflow relative to permanentLockBalance, griefing or stealing rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute `permanentLockBalance` explicitly on multiSplit by subtracting the original permanent amount and adding each new NFT's amount; ensure exact-sum allocation (give the last share the remainder) to preserve invariants.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow multiSplit leaves permanentLockBalance out of sync allowing reward dilution
hypotheses.description: `multiSplit` burns the source veNFT and creates new ones with amounts `int128(uint256(int256(originalLocked.amount)) * amounts[i] / totalWeight)`. Integer truncation means the sum of new amounts can be less than the original amount. `permanentLockBalance` is NOT modified in `multiSplit`, so it stays equal to the original permanent amount even though the locked sum across new NFTs is smaller (round-down loss) or — if any share rounds to zero — an NFT is created with zero amount yet counted as a permanent holder path through `_checkpoint` where `_tokenId != 0` and `new_locked.isPermanent` is true, setting `u_new.permanent = 0` in user point history but global `point_history.permanent = permanentLockBalance` (over counting). Over repeated splits, `permanentLockBalance` (and hence `point_history[last].permanent`, which feeds `totalSupplyAtT`) drifts above the true sum of locked amounts. `RewardsDistributor` divides `tokens_per_week` by `totalSupplyAtT`, so an inflated total supply under-pays every other veNFT holder.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains (or creates) a permanent veNFT of amount N. 2) Attacker calls `multiSplit(_from, [1, 1])` (or any weights where `N * w_i / totalWeight` truncates). New tokens sum to N-k for k ≥ 0 and `permanentLockBalance` remains N (unchanged). 3) The new NFTs' histories push `point_history[_epoch].permanent = permanentLockBalance = N`. 4) `totalSupplyAtT` under-reports the true sum of locked balances because it uses `point_history.permanent` as the base when the lock is permanent. 5) Repeated `multiSplit` calls further inflate the discrepancy. 6) Attacker then claims from `RewardsDistributor`; because total supply is inflated, the attacker's own share (which uses the NFT's real, smaller amount via `balanceOfNFTAt`) — wait, the attacker also benefits from the inflation in reward share? Actually a higher totalSupply reduces each NFT's share of the fixed `tokens_per_week`, so all users get less — but the attacker may not gain directly. The gain is that `claim` in RewardsDistributor calls `deposit_for(_tokenId, amount)` for non-expired NFTs, which increases the attacker's locked amount "for free" while `permanentLockBalance` (and thus totalSupply) is only incremented by the deposit amount — no, deposit_for increments `permanentLockBalance` only if isPermanent. So the attacker gets extra HYBR locked but doesn't break the invariant further. Attacker's real gain is short-changed for others while attacker's veNFT remains the same weight, so attacker's absolute reward per epoch is unchanged but every other user's reward is reduced → for other users it's a griefing attack. More importantly, `unlockPermanent` on the new NFT subtracts `_amount` from `permanentLockBalance`, which was left at the old larger N. If the attacker previously inflated by k, calling `unlockPermanent` reduces `permanentLockBalance` by `_amount` (the new NFT's actual amount), so `permanentLockBalance` ends at N - newamount which is > actual sum of permanent locks → still inflated but recoverable. Properly crafted sequences let the attacker mint HYBR via RewardsDistributor claims where balance is paid as a deposit_for — attacker can in practice profit by turning rebase rewards into larger locked positions and wait for expiry. Iterated, this leads to HYBR misallocation.
hypotheses.impact: Total supply miscalculation affects RewardsDistributor shares for all veNFT holders; can be repeated to systematically skew reward distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute `permanentLockBalance` in `multiSplit` by subtracting the original permanent amount and adding each new NFT's permanent amount, and assign the remainder to one share so amounts sum exactly to the original.

hypotheses.title: collectProtocolFees decrements amount before transfer, skips if amount==1
hypotheses.description: The function uses `uint128(amount0)` as-is, but transfers `--amount0`, and only does so when `amount0 > 0`. When `protocolFees.token0 == 1`, `--amount0` yields 0, transfer of 0 tokens is made, and accrued 1-wei fee balances accumulate forever. More importantly, because there is no check on whether `msg.sender == factory` beyond the require and no check that the protocol-fee slot resets correctly when reentered during the transfer, the storage update order (`protocolFees.token0 = 0` before transfer) is fine, but the `--amount0` pattern silently reduces the transferred amount by 1 relative to the balance snapshot, so protocol accounting drifts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (any caller can be routed via factory only) — but any pool with accrued protocol fees notices that the very last wei is never retrievable. This is a state consistency defect rather than a direct theft: over many pools the accumulated 1-wei remains stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Trivial loss of protocol funds (1 wei per pool per token) and misleading emitted events (amount0 returns 0 though 1 wei sits in `protocolFees`).
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `amount0 = protocolFees.token0; protocolFees.token0 = 0; TransferHelper.safeTransfer(token0, recipient, amount0);` without the `--` and without the `> 1` guard.

hypotheses.title: GrowthHYBR.withdraw uses multiSplit with three shares that can mis-map
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` calls `multiSplit(veTokenId, [remainingAmount, userAmount, feeAmount])`. `multiSplit` creates new veNFTs proportional to the inputs' weights (`amounts[i] / totalWeight`). Here the three weights are token amounts (HYBR units), so the resulting new veNFTs will each hold `originalLocked.amount * weight_i / totalWeight`. If `originalLocked.amount != remaining + userAmount + feeAmount` (e.g., because `totalAssets()` returns the actual locked amount at call time and the contract also holds additional HYBR to be compounded, or because earlier `deposit_for` roundings), then `newTokenIds[0]` (which becomes the contract's new `veTokenId`) ends up holding a different HYBR amount than intended. In particular `userAmount`/`feeAmount` are computed after fee, but `multiSplit` weights are the raw token amounts; summing `remaining + userAmount + feeAmount` may not equal `originalLocked.amount`, so the new contract veNFT is under/over-funded versus gHYBR's totalSupply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Depositor deposits an amount. 2) Another deposit extracts tiny rounding dust, making `totalAssets()` exceed `remaining + userAmount + feeAmount`. 3) Withdrawer calls `withdraw(shares)`; weights under-sum, so `newTokenIds[0]` receives less than `remaining`, which under-collateralizes the remaining gHYBR holders. Rounding repeated across users compounds value leak.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution/theft of HYBR from remaining gHYBR holders; the contract's veNFT balance diverges from `totalSupply()` leading to broken `calculateShares`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `originalLocked.amount` as the base for all three splits so the weights sum exactly (`weights = [remaining, userAmount, feeAmount]` scaled to `originalLocked.amount`), or derive the remaining weight from `originalLocked.amount - userAmount - feeAmount`.

hypotheses.title: calculateFees miscalculates staked share when liquidity == stakedLiquidity
hypotheses.description: In `calculateFees`, when `_liquidity == _stakedLiquidity` (i.e. all liquidity is staked), the entire `feeAmount` is assigned to `stakedFeeAmount` and `feeGrowthGlobalX128` stays 0. However the same logic is used for `flash` where `_liquidity` is the pool-wide `liquidity` but staked fee accrual should still not bypass unstaked fee / protocol fee per factory settings. Worse, in the `else if (_stakedLiquidity == 0)` branch, `applyUnstakedFees(feeAmount, 0)` is called and the resulting `_protocolFeeAmount` / `_stakedFeeAmount` are taken from `applyUnstakedFees`, but they are returned from a function that only computes `_protocolFee` when `protocolFee() > 0`; when `protocolFee() == 0` the code computes an `unstakedFee()` levy instead and takes `_stakedFee` from the unstaked amount. `gaugeFees` therefore accrues fee from unstaked LPs' share while `feeGrowthGlobalX128` is computed on the reduced `unstakedFeeAmount`, but the fee split basis is `_liquidity`, not `_liquidity - _stakedLiquidity`. In a pool where staked liquidity exists but the current tick has zero staked liquidity (e.g., staked position is out of range), `_stakedLiquidity == 0` at that instant, so `applyUnstakedFees` sends part of the fee to the gauge that has no staked liquidity in range. This causes staked LPs to not receive rewards and unstaked LPs to subsidize gauge fee accrual disproportionately.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker creates a staked position out of range (tick range below current tick) and a large unstaked position in range. Every swap produces `_stakedLiquidity == 0`, so `applyUnstakedFees` with `_stakedFee = mulDivRoundingUp(unstakedFeeAmount, unstakedFee(), 1e6)` routes a portion to `gaugeFees` even though no staked liquidity is in range to earn it. The gauge owner (also attacker) later calls `collectFees()` and captures the fee.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge receives fees not backed by staked liquidity; unstaked LPs earn less than they should; protocol accounting drifts from real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Determine staked in-range liquidity from the tick-crossing state, not from `_stakedLiquidity` computation in `calculateFees`; only charge `unstakedFee` when there is genuinely staked liquidity in range.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL._earned overcounts reward when lastUpdateTime is stale
hypotheses.description: `_earned(tokenId)` uses `clPool.lastUpdated()` to project `rewardGrowthGlobalX128` forward for the elapsed `timeDelta`, but then adds the projection to the pool's CURRENT `rewardGrowthGlobalX128`. In `CLPool._updateRewardsGrowthGlobal`, `lastUpdated` is updated only when `timeDelta != 0`, and `rewardReserve` is decremented inside that call. Between two calls in the same block, `timeDelta` is 0. However GaugeCL's `_earned` is a view and does not gate on `lastUpdateTime[tokenId] == block.timestamp`. If a user stakes, then in the same block another user stakes, `_updateRewards` for the second user sees `lastUpdateTime[secondUser] == 0` (or old) and projects `reward = rewardRate * timeDelta` even though the pool already advanced `lastUpdated`. In particular, when `rewardRate` is updated by `notifyRewardAmount` mid-epoch, `lastUpdateTime` is not reset for existing stakers, causing them to be credited rewards for time before the rate change was applied.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker stakes right before `notifyRewardAmount` is called in a new epoch. Because pool's `lastUpdated` earlier already advanced (for the previous epoch's sync), the attacker's position captures `rewardGrowthInside` delta from before their deposit, then `_earned` again adds elapsed-time rewards since `lastUpdated` inside `GaugeCL`, effectively double-counting reward across the epoch boundary. Withdraw immediately with `redeemType=0` to convert at the maximum rate.
hypotheses.impact: Over-reward to attacker; under-reward to honest stakers; drain of `rewardReserve` faster than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_earned`, treat `rewardGrowthGlobalX128` as the pool's stored value when `clPool.lastUpdated() == clPool._blockTimestamp`, and always call `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` before computing earned.

hypotheses.title: NonfungiblePositionManager.increaseLiquidity ignores slippage when staked
hypotheses.description: When the position is staked (`isStaked == true`), `addLiquidity` is called with `recipient: gauge`, and the `amount0Min`/`amount1Min` checks inside `addLiquidity` still apply. However, the caller-supplied `params.amount0Min`/`params.amount1Min` are passed through, but the function does not verify that the resulting `liquidity` is non-zero or that the amounts are within any bound relative to the desired amounts beyond the min checks. More importantly, for staked positions the fee-growth update is skipped (`if (!isStaked)`), so `position.tokensOwed0/1` are not credited; the gauge's position is updated instead. A caller who increases liquidity on a staked position via the gauge can have their `amount0Min`/`amount1Min` satisfied while the actual liquidity added is minimal (e.g., due to a price move between quote and execution), and the position's `liquidity` is incremented by the returned `liquidity` without any additional check.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `increaseLiquidity` for a staked position. 2) Attacker moves the pool price so that `getLiquidityForAmounts` returns a much smaller `liquidity` for the same desired amounts. 3) The victim's `amount0Min`/`amount1Min` are still satisfied (since less liquidity means less of each token is used), but the victim receives far less liquidity than expected. 4) Attacker reverses the price move.
hypotheses.impact: Victims receive less liquidity than expected for their deposited tokens; value extracted by the attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `liquidityMin` parameter to `increaseLiquidity` and require `liquidity >= liquidityMin`, or enforce a minimum liquidity relative to the desired amounts.

hypotheses.title: Bribe.getReward loops over caller-supplied tokens array, gas griefing on claim
hypotheses.description: `getReward(tokenId, tokens)` iterates over the caller-supplied `tokens` array and calls `earned(tokenId, tokens[i])` for each. `earned` itself loops up to `numEpochs` (bounded by time since last claim) and performs binary searches. A caller (via `GaugeManager.claimBribes` / `claimAllBribes`) can pass an arbitrarily large `tokens` array, causing the transaction to run out of gas. While this only affects the caller's own transaction, `GaugeManager.claimAllBribes` iterates over `_bribes` and `_nftIds` arrays supplied by the caller, and a malicious `_bribes` entry pointing to a contract that reverts or consumes gas can block the entire claim loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `GaugeManager.claimAllBribes` with a `_bribes` array containing a malicious contract that reverts in `getReward`. 2) The loop reverts, so the attacker's own claim fails — but if this is used by a keeper or aggregator, it blocks batch claims. 3) Alternatively, a large `tokens` array causes OOG.
hypotheses.impact: Batch bribe claims can be griefed; keepers/aggregators cannot process claims for multiple users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound the `tokens` array length, or wrap each `IBribe.getReward` call in try/catch in `GaugeManager.claimAllBribes`.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL stake/unstake double-counting allows reward inflation via repeated deposit
hypotheses.description: `deposit` calls `clPool.stake(int128(liquidity), tickLower, tickUpper, true)` which increases `stakedLiquidity` in the pool by the NFT's liquidity, and stores `_stakes[msg.sender].add(tokenId)`. The pool has no record of which NFT's liquidity is already staked: it trusts the delta passed in. Because the NFT is transferred to the gauge via `safeTransferFrom`, the same token cannot be re-deposited by the original owner... but the pool's `stakedLiquidity` accounting is global and the reward pool pays out pro-rata. The `stake` function updates `stakedLiquidity` based only on the passed delta and the current tick in range; there is no check that the delta corresponds to the NFT's actual liquidity. A user can `withdraw` (which calls `stake(-liquidityToStake, ..., true)` if `liquidityToStake != 0`) and the NFT is returned, then re-`deposit`. Between deposit and withdraw, `_earned` accrues based on `stakedLiquidity` global; but the pool's `stakedLiquidity` never decreases if `liquidityToStake == 0` (user decreased liquidity to zero before withdrawing). The user then still holds an NFT with zero liquidity, withdraws (skips the stake(-delta) due to the `if (liquidityToStake != 0)` guard), and the pool's `stakedLiquidity` remains inflated while real liquidity is gone. Other stakers are diluted.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User stakes NFT with small liquidity L0 via gauge.deposit. 2) User (through gauge, as owner) calls `increaseLiquidity` repeatedly, growing the position to L1 >> L0. Each increaseLiquidity routes through NFT manager: `addLiquidity` -> `pool.mint(recipient=gauge, ...)` which increases `position.liquidity` and pool `liquidity`, but never calls `pool.stake`, so `stakedLiquidity` remains L0-base. 3) Wait for reward growth. 4) Call `gauge.withdraw(tokenId)`: `_getReward` computes `rewardGrowthInside[tokenId]` delta * (large L1) / Q128, paying roughly L1/L0 times more rewards than the user's actual staked contribution. 5) Reward reserve is drained faster than intended; other stakers receive less.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of rewardReserve, dilution of other stakers' rewards, broken accounting between stakedLiquidity and real liquidity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have `GaugeCL` call `clPool.stake` after any position liquidity change, or track the position's liquidity on deposit/stake and reconcile on every reward update so rewards use only the currently-staked liquidity.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL._updateRewards can double-count rewards for token added before lastUpdated reset
hypotheses.description: `_updateRewards` sets `lastUpdateTime[tokenId] = block.timestamp` and then calls `_earned` which uses `clPool.lastUpdated()` to compute the accrual window. However `_earned` reads `clPool.rewardGrowthGlobalX128()` and `clPool.rewardReserve()`, and re-derives the reward-growth inside using a freshly-requested `rewardGrowthGlobalX128` — but `getRewardGrowthInside(tickLower, tickUpper, 0)` uses `0` as sentinel to read the live global. Between `_updateRewards` and the subsequent `_getReward` call in a second tx, the update sequence is not idempotent: if the pool's `lastUpdated` equals `block.timestamp` (because someone else called `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` in the same block), the timeDelta is 0 so the gauge's `rewards[tokenId]` snapshot is not refreshed while `rewardGrowthInside[tokenId]` is updated — then on the next `_earned` for a different path, `rewardGrowthInside[tokenId]` is smaller than the actual current value, causing `rewardPerTokenInsideX128 - rewardPerTokenInsideInitialX128` to be over-counted and double-paying.
hypotheses.attackPath: A depositor times deposit/withdraw across a block where `updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` was already called by the minter/distribution path so `clPool.lastUpdated == block.timestamp`. 2) Calling `deposit` then `withdraw` (or `getReward`) in successive blocks panics the internal `rewardGrowthInside` snapshot relative to global growth, extracting more reward than accrued.
hypotheses.impact: Reward token over-drain from the gauge (rewards paid twice); potential insolvency of the gauge's rHYBR conversion path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute and store the global `rewardGrowthGlobalX128` in a single call path, using the returned updated value rather than re-reading `clPool.getRewardGrowthInside(..., 0)` after storing `rewards[tokenId]`.

hypotheses.title: Bribe.notifyRewardAmount credits current-epoch start without checking minter active_period
hypotheses.description: `earned()` computes rewards per epoch keyed on `HybraTimeLibrary.epochStart(block.timestamp)`, while `getEpochStart()` returns `IMinter(minter).active_period()`. These values can diverge (minter's `active_period` is set one week ahead at init and rolls forward on weekly update; `epochStart` uses the raw week boundary). `notifyRewardAmount` credits `tokenRewardsPerEpoch[_rewardsToken][HybraTimeLibrary.epochStart(block.timestamp)]`, but if the minter has not yet performed `update_period()` for the week, the voters’ `lastEarn` for that epoch resolves via `getPriorBalanceIndex` and `getPriorSupplyIndex`, and the divergence causes rewards to be missed or double-counted for the current week.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker waits for the first block after a weekly boundary but before `Minter.update_period()` is called. Attacker calls `Bribe.notifyRewardAmount` (allowed on the internal bribe via GaugeCL claim flow) crediting the new epoch start. `earned()` iterates from `epochStart(lastEarn)`; if the voter/minters timing is skewed (e.g., the minter drifts because `_initializer != address(0)`), for that same boundary users can claim from the previous epoch's checkpoint at the new epoch key, effectively double-spending the bribe.
hypotheses.impact: Bribes paid to wrong epochs → honest voters see reduced rewards; reward double-claims possible; `totalSupply`/checkpoint drift.
hypotheses.recommendation: Align Bribe's epoch accounting with `IMinter(minter).active_period()` directly instead of `epochStart(block.timestamp)`.

hypotheses.title: RewardHYBR._redeemToGHYBR double-calls gHYBR with incorrect penalty accounting
hypotheses.description: `_redeemToGHYBR` approves `gHYBR` for `amount` and calls `IGHYBR(gHYBR).deposit(amount, recipient)`. But the token flow is: user burns `amount` rHYBR, then `gHYBR.deposit` pulls `amount` HYBR from this contract via `transferFrom`. HYBR balance is only guaranteed if HYBR was previously transferred in for `deposit` of rHYBR. However for `TO_HYBR` path the penalty portion is transferred to `gHYBR` via `safeTransfer(gHYBR, penalty)` and then `receivePenaltyReward(penalty)` is called, which also calls `deposit_for` — those HYBR tokens are pulled twice from this contract (once from `safeTransfer(gHYBR, penalty)` and once inside `receivePenaltyReward` via `transferFrom`), and this can revert or over-credit `penalty` in GrowthHYBR since `receivePenaltyReward` uses whatever HYBR is already at gHYBR (not necessarily transferred via the prior `safeTransfer`).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `redeem(amount, 0)` (TO_HYBR). The transaction does `safeTransfer(HYBR, gHYBR, penalty)` then `gHYBR.receivePenaltyReward(penalty)`. GrowthHYBR then does `transferFrom(address(this), ...)` requiring rHYBR to have transferred HYBR to GrowthHYBR, which it did. But the `safeTransfer` in RewardHYBR sent HYBR to gHYBR (GrowthHYBR), which then pulls again from address(this) via `approve`+`transferFrom`. Any user redeeming can cause the second transferFrom to fail or double-count penalty, potentially locking funds sent to GrowthHYBR.
hypotheses.impact: Potential revert / stuck tokens; GrowthHYBR's `penalty` accounting may not equal transferred HYBR.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not `safeTransfer(HYBR, gHYBR, penalty)` before `receivePenaltyReward`; instead rely on a single top-up flow that atomically pulls the penalty from RewardHYBR's HYBR balance.

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL.withdraw switches msg.sender ownership checks after collect
hypotheses.description: `withdraw(tokenId, redeemType)` requires `_stakes[msg.sender].contains(tokenId)` but then calls `nonfungiblePositionManager.collect` with `recipient: msg.sender`, and later `nonfungiblePositionManager.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId)`. During `collect`, the pool's `_collect` on the staked path uses `owner: gauge` and forwards to `recipient` which is `msg.sender`. That is fine for the owner, but `collect` triggers `pool.burn(..., 0, gauge)` and then the gauge's position is updated. If `msg.sender` is not the actual owner of the underlying NFT (because `_stakes` mapping was keyed by whoever staked), an attacker who transferred the NFT to the gauge but never was in `_stakes` can call `getReward` via the distribution path only if listed. The direct `withdraw` path requires the stake record, but an attacker can use `GaugeManager.claimRewards(address[] _gauges, ...)` calling `IGauge(_gauges[i]).getReward(msg.sender, _redeemType)` for the classic gauge. For CL gauges, `GaugeManager.claimRewards(address _gauge, uint256[] _nftIds, uint8 _redeemType)` calls `IGaugeCL(_gauge).getReward(_nftIds[i], msg.sender, _redeemType)` which requires `_stakes[account].contains(tokenId)`. So the routing is consistent. The bug is the reverse: `withdraw` allows withdraw when `liquidityToStake != 0` triggers `clPool.stake(-int128(liquidityToStake), tickLower, tickUpper, true)` — but the pool's stakedLiquidity accounting uses the gauge's tracked amount, which may drift if the user manipulates liquidity between staking and unstaking. If a user increases position liquidity while staked (via NonfungiblePositionManager.increaseLiquidity with `recipient: gauge`), the gauge's `_stakes` record is not updated, but on withdraw the gauge unstakes only the current `liquidityToStake` from the positions() call. `stakedLiquidity` on the pool then goes negative relative to actual stake if `int128(liquidityToStake)` exceeds the amount previously staked.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker stakes a position, then calls `increaseLiquidity` via NFPM (which allows `msg.sender == gauge` path) to add liquidity. `clPool.stake` is called with the delta on the pool for the gauge's position. On withdrawal, `_stakes` set is removed and `clPool.stake(-int128(liquidityToStake), ...)` is called with the full new liquidity. The pool's `stakedLiquidity` may be manipulated since the increase wasn't mirrored in the gauge's stake call.
hypotheses.impact: `stakedLiquidity` accounting drifts; reward growth per staked liquidity is miscomputed; LPs receive wrong rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the originally-staked liquidity per tokenId in the gauge and always unstake exactly that amount (or call into the pool's actual staked liquidity state).

hypotheses.title: GaugeCL.notifyRewardAmount double-counts rollover in rewardReserve
hypotheses.description: `totalRewardAmount = rewardAmount + clPool.rollover()` is passed as `rewardReserve` to `clPool.syncReward`, but `rollover` is also accumulated inside the pool's `_updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` when `stakedLiquidity == 0`. If `notifyRewardAmount` is called while `stakedLiquidity == 0`, the rollover is added to the reserve, and then the pool's own `_updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` (called at the start of `notifyRewardAmount`) may add the same rollover again on the next update, effectively double-counting the reserve and allowing more rewards to be distributed than were actually funded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until `stakedLiquidity == 0` and a rollover has accumulated. 2) Attacker (as GaugeManager, but the condition is reachable via normal operation) triggers `notifyRewardAmount`; the rollover is added to `rewardReserve`. 3) Subsequent `_updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` calls re-add the rollover, inflating the reserve. 4) Attacker stakes and harvests to extract the inflated rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of rHYBR; gauge/pool reward reserve is drained faster than funded.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not add `clPool.rollover()` to `rewardReserve` in `notifyRewardAmount`; let the pool's `_updateRewardsGrowthGlobal` handle rollover exclusively, or reset `rollover` to zero when consuming it.

hypotheses.title: CLLFactory.getSwapFee trusts malicious fee-module return
hypotheses.description: `getSwapFee` calls `swapFeeModule.excessivelySafeStaticCall(...)` and trusts the decoded uint24 as long as `fee <= 100_000`. Because `swapFeeModule` is upgradeable via `setSwapFeeModule` and is called on every swap path through `CLPool.fee()`, a module that returns an artificially inflated (yet ≤ 100000) fee extracts extra value from every swap while appearing legitimate. The pool performs no sanity check that the returned fee matches what the module actually advertised through its events, nor is `getUnstakedFee`/`getProtocolFee` similarly constrained across the same module state.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a benign-looking fee module that returns 100000 (10%) regardless of pool; governance-set module only via swapFeeManager — if that path ever uses external calls or is set to an upgradable-proxy pattern, an external actor can be made recipient of the fee. In-scope for integrated state: the pool trusts the module's return value verbatim and applies it on every swap, whereas the module is a separate contract potentially updated without pool cooperation.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic over-charging of swap fees; wrong accounting between staked/unstaked split (splitFees/applyUnstakedFees uses the same fee) leading to mismatch with emitted `Swap` fees and actual token movements.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cross-check the returned fee against `tickSpacingToFee[pool.tickSpacing()]` (or a max delta), and validate `swapFeeModule` interface stability via immutable snapshot rather than re-reading storage each call.
